rationale: A wins because it knows where the land mines are and turns them into usable strategy, especially "Toast wants to be its restaurants' bank. It won't say how many of them default." B has good bones, but it flinches from the accountability story by refusing "Toast responds to fee criticism" as merely a "standing vulnerability" when the update hands it undisclosed defaults plus fee complaints. A is more distinct, better gated, and more useful to a founder who needs to know what not to pitch as much as what to pitch.
gaps_in_A: "The restaurant POS is becoming the restaurant's bank" is directionally smart, but it leans on a category claim from one company's facts; A admits the weakness, but it is still the softest kept angle.
"Toast's path to profit runs through lending" slightly overstates causality. The facts say Toast reached profitability and says fintech is higher-margin, not that lending caused profitability.
"How one restaurant repaid its POS provider a slice of every day's sales" only works if a named borrower exists. Without that operator, it is a placeholder, not yet a story.
gaps_in_B: "underwritten by the payment flow Toast already sees" invents underwriting mechanics. The update says Toast processes sales and repayment is tied to daily sales; it does not say underwriting uses that data.
"Toast got profitable by selling money, not hardware" overstates the supplied facts. Higher-margin fintech plus recent profitability is not proof that financial services drove profitability.
Refusing "Toast responds to fee criticism" as "no_why_now_but_required" is the wrong call. Bundling lending into the platform is exactly why fee complaints and undisclosed defaults become timely.
"four viable shapes exist across three distinct beats" is generous; the first and fourth angles both orbit the same embedded-finance/margin-mix story and need sharper separation.
